Creditor
KRED-i-tor
noun
From the Latin creditor, one who trusts or lends, from credere, to believe or entrust; in Scripture the man to whom a debt is owed, holding a claim upon the debtor’s goods, land, and even his person.

Biblical Definition

A creditor is one who has lent and to whom repayment is owed. Scripture neither forbids lending nor treats the creditor’s claim as unjust; it hedges his claim about with mercy. Every seventh year the release was proclaimed: “Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD’S release” (Deu 15:2). The debt was real, and the remission was real, and the ground of the remission was the character of God, not the poverty of the borrower. Where that law was neglected the creditor’s power became terrible, as in the prophet’s widow who cried to Elisha that “the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen” (2Ki 4:1) — and God answered her not by cancelling the debt but by multiplying oil until she could pay it and live on the rest. Solomon states the plain sociology: “the borrower is servant to the lender” (Pro 22:7). Our Lord takes the whole figure into the doctrine of forgiveness. To Simon the Pharisee He set two debtors of one creditor, five hundred pence and fifty, neither able to pay, both frankly forgiven, and asked which would love him most (Luk 7:41–42). Simon judged rightly, and condemned himself in judging: the woman washing Christ’s feet with tears knew the size of her debt. Little love is the mark, not of little sin, but of little sense of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

One to whom a debt is due; in Scripture a lawful office bounded by the seventh-year release, and Christ’s figure for the God who frankly forgives.

expand to see more

CREDITOR, n. [L. creditor, from credere, to trust.] A person to whom a sum of money or other thing is due, by obligation, promise or in law.

Opposed to debtor; in book-keeping, the side on which payments received are entered.

In the Mosaic law the creditor’s claim was released in the seventh year (Deu 15:2).

He might not take the widow’s raiment nor the millstone to pledge (Deu 24:6, 17).

Figuratively, one who has a just claim of any kind upon another.

Key Scripture

Deu 15:2 — "And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD'S release."

2Ki 4:1 — "Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets unto Elisha, saying, Thy servant my husband is dead; and thou knowest that thy servant did fear the LORD: and the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen."

Luk 7:41 — "There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty."

Luk 7:42 — "And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?"

Modern Corruption

The parable of the two debtors is preached as an encouragement to forgive ourselves and one another, with the creditor’s real claim and the reason for the greater love quietly dropped.

expand to see more

The corruption is the softening of the debt. Modern preaching often treats forgiveness as the release of a grudge — something the offended party does for his own peace — and reads Luk 7 as a lesson in generosity of spirit. But the parable turns on a sum that was genuinely owed and genuinely unpayable: “when they had nothing to pay.” God does not forgive by pretending the account is small; He forgives by having the account settled in the blood of His Son, so that the remission is both free to us and costly to Him. Strip the debt of its reality and the woman’s tears become sentiment, Simon’s coldness becomes a personality trait, and the gospel becomes God’s decision to overlook. The other error runs the opposite way: a creditor’s religion which presses the last farthing from a brother while pleading grace for itself — the unmerciful servant of Mat 18, forgiven ten thousand talents and taking his fellow by the throat for a hundred pence.

Recover the arithmetic of love. He to whom much is forgiven loveth much; and the man who thinks his own debt was fifty pence will love little and serve coldly, however orthodox his profession. Recover also the seventh-year mercy in its own sphere. The release was not the abolition of lending but the refusal to let a brother be ground permanently into bondage by his obligations — the same instinct that would not take a widow’s garment in pledge. Lend honestly, keep your word, pay what you owe; and when you hold a claim over a brother whom God has already forgiven ten thousand talents, remember whose release it is called.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

One to whom a debt is due; hedged by the LORD’S release, and made by Christ the picture of the God who forgives what could never be paid.

expand to see more

Creditor — Latin creditor, from credere, to trust or entrust.

Hebrew nashah / baal mashsheh yad, the master of the loan of the hand (Deu 15:2).

Greek daneistes, the money-lender of the parable (Luk 7:41).

The seventh-year release is called the LORD’S, not the borrower’s (Deu 15:2).

Elisha’s widow: the creditor’s lawful claim answered by God’s provision, not by default.

Usage

"Scripture regulates the creditor; it does not abolish lending or excuse the debtor."

"The two-debtor parable measures love by the sense of the debt forgiven, not by temperament."

"“Nothing to pay” is the state of every sinner before God — the only qualification for free remission."
